<p><strong>Written by Ken Huang, CEO at <a href="http://distributedapps.ai">DistributedApps.ai</a> and Jerry Huang, Engineering Fellow, Kleiner Perkins.</strong></p>

<p> </p>

<h2 style="font-size:2.2em;font-weight:400;">Abstract</h2>

<p>AI agents used in e-commerce necessitates secure payment protocols capable of handling high-determinism user authorization, agent authentication, and non-repudiable accountability. The Agent Payments Protocol (AP2) [1], an open extension to Agent2Agent (A2A) [2] and Model Context Protocol (MCP) [3], introduces Verifiable Credentials (VCs) in the form of cryptographically signed Mandates to establish trust without relying solely on probabilistic AI inferences. This blog provides a detailed security analysis of AP2, elucidating its role-based architecture, cryptographic primitives (e.g., ECDSA signatures [12]), and transaction flows for both human-present and human-not-present modalities. We identify vulnerabilities such as mandate spoofing and agent coercion, proposing mitigations including hardware-backed key management and decentralized allowlists. Guidelines for secure implementation include integration with Strong Customer Authentication (SCA) [7], configuration of Intent Mandate TTLs, and dispute resolution protocols. The expanded analysis draws from AP2's specification, reference implementations in Python and Android, and aligns with standards like W3C VCs [4]. Recommendations emphasize practicality, enabling developers to deploy AP2 safely while fostering agentic commerce innovation.</p>

<p> </p>

<h2 style="font-size:2.2em;font-weight:400;">Introduction</h2>

<h3 style="font-size:1.8em;font-weight:700;">Background and Motivation</h3>

<p>Traditional payment systems are architected around human-mediated interactions, where user authentication occurs in real-time via trusted interfaces (e.g., merchant websites or native apps). With the advent of AI agents—powered by LLMs like Gemini 2.5, Claude, GPT5, etc and orchestrated via protocols like A2A and MCP—transactions may involve minimal or zero user supervision. Agents can autonomously browse catalogs, negotiate terms, bundle purchases across merchants, and execute payments, introducing unprecedented convenience but also novel security challenges [1]:</p>

<ul>
	<li><strong>Authorization Gaps:</strong> How to verifiably delegate authority without exposing payment methods? Conventional OAuth flows assume synchronous user presence.</li>
	<li><strong>Authenticity Risks:</strong> AI "hallucinations" [5] could lead to erroneous purchases; how to anchor transactions to explicit user intent?</li>
	<li><strong>Liability Ambiguities:</strong> If a transaction fails or is disputed, who bears responsibility—the user, the agent's developer, or the merchant?</li>
</ul>

<p>These issues undermine trust, potentially fragmenting the ecosystem into proprietary, siloed solutions. Existing attempts to bolt-on agent support (e.g., via enhanced APIs) fail to provide the required cryptographic assurances and have led to increased fraud rates in early simulations [10].</p>

<p>AP2 addresses this by reimagining payments as "contractual conversations" [1], where VCs serve as signed contracts. These mandates are portable, tamper-evident, and verifiable across parties, ensuring non-repudiable proof of intent.</p>

<h2 style="font-size:2.2em;font-weight:400;">Related Work</h2>

<h3 style="font-size:1.8em;font-weight:700;">Agent Protocols and Trust Establishment</h3>

<p>A2A [2] enables secure message passing between agents, employing TLS-based encryption and agent card-based identity. MCP [3] adds resource abstraction for tool access, but neither natively supports financial primitives. AP2 extends these by defining payment-specific VCs, leveraging W3C VC standards [4] for schema alignment and DID-based verification [9].</p>

<p>Research in AI agent security [5, 6] highlights channel vulnerabilities in delegated systems. For instance, man-in-the-middle attacks on LLM-tool pipelines can alter intent. AP2's use of signed mandates counters this by requiring deterministic user approval, aligning with multi-party computation principles [6].</p>

<p> </p>

<h3 style="font-size:1.8em;font-weight:700;">Payment Security and Cryptographic Innovations</h3>

<p>Modern payments integrate SCA [7], which mandates dynamic linking of authentication to transaction details. AP2's Cart Mandate incorporates this by including full transaction payloads in signatures. PCI-DSS [11] influences role segregation in AP2, ensuring CPs handle tokens separately from SAs.</p>

<p>Decentralized credentials [9] inform AP2's trust anchors, with issuers (e.g., card providers) as roots of trust. However, AP2 innovates by adding "agent modality" signals to Payment Mandates, enabling new risk models [18].</p>

<p>Comparisons to other protocols: RIPPLE's blockchain-based payments [14] offers similar auditability but lacks AP2's lightweight, non-blockchain dependency for agent orchestration.</p>

<h2 style="font-size:2.2em;font-weight:400;">AP2 Architecture</h2>

<h3 style="font-size:1.8em;font-weight:700;">Role-Based Design and Interactions</h3>

<p>AP2's ecosystem distributes responsibilities to prevent single points of failure (Fig. 1). Agents communicate via A2A/MCP channels.</p>

<ul>
	<li><strong>User (U):</strong> Human entity; provides initial prompts and final authorizations.</li>
	<li><strong>Shopping Agent (SA/U):</strong> Root agent (e.g., powered by Google ADK), delegates to sub-agents for collection (products, shipping, payment). Example Python code from AP2 samples [1]:</li>
</ul>

<p><code>root_agent = RetryingLlmAgent(</code></p>

<p><code>    model="gemini-2.5-flash",</code></p>

<p><code>    instruction="... [orchestrates purchase flow]",</code></p>

<p><code>    tools=[tools.create_payment_mandate, tools.initiate_payment],</code></p>

<p><code>    sub_agents=[shopper, payment_method_collector]  # Delegation example</code></p>

<p><code>)</code></p>

<ul>
	<li><strong>Credentials Provider (CP):</strong> Manages payment methods; e.g., tokenizes Visa cards via issuer APIs [1].</li>
	<li><strong>Merchant Endpoint (ME):</strong> Negotiates carts; signs Merchant-Signed Cart Mandates for fulfillment assurances.</li>
	<li><strong>Merchant Payment Processor (MPP):</strong> Aggregates mandates into issuer-ready messages.</li>
	<li><strong>Network/Issuer:</strong> Processes payments; uses Payment Mandate signals for AI-aware risk scoring [1].</li>
</ul>

<h3 style="font-size:1.8em;font-weight:700;">Verifiable Credentials and Mandates</h3>

<p>Mandates are JSON-LD objects [4] with cryptographic signatures (ECDSA [12]) for integrity. Core schema from <code>src/ap2/types/mandate.py</code> [1]:</p>

<p><code>class CartMandate(BaseModel):</code></p>

<p><code>    contents: CartContents  # Items, prices, payment method token</code></p>

<p><code>    merchant_signature: str  # Sig_ME(contents)</code></p>

<p><code>    timestamp: datetime</code></p>

<p><code>class IntentMandate(BaseModel):</code></p>

<p><code>    contents: IntentContents  # Constraints: category, budget, TTL</code></p>

<p><code>    user_signature: str  # Sig_U(contents) on-device</code></p>

<p><code>    timestamp: datetime</code></p>

<ul>
	<li><strong>Cart Mandate:</strong> Human-present; ME provides, U signs. Payload:

	<ul>
		<li>Payer/Payee IDs (e.g., DIDs [9]).</li>
		<li>Tokenized payment method.</li>
		<li>Risk signals (IMEI, location).</li>
		<li>Exact transaction details (total, shipping via PaymentCurrencyAmount class).</li>
	</ul>
	</li>
	<li><strong>Intent Mandate:</strong> Human-not-present; SA creates, U signs. Adds "prompt playback" (NLP summary of user intent) and TTL for temporal limits.</li>
	<li><strong>Payment Mandate:</strong> Derived from Cart/Intent; sent to issuer. Signals: Human-Present/Not-Present, agent ID. Schema from src/ap2/types/mandate.py:</li>
</ul>

<p><code>class PaymentMandate(BaseModel):</code></p>

<p><code>    payment_details: PaymentMandateContents  # Hashed Cart/Intent, method, amount</code></p>

<p><code>    creation_time: datetime</code></p>

<p>Signatures use hardware keys (e.g., Android DPC [21]); verification via public key chains [9].</p>

<p> </p>

<h3 style="font-size:1.8em;font-weight:700;">Transaction Flows</h3>

<p><strong>Human-Present Flow</strong></p>

<ol>
	<li>U → SA: "Buy shoes."</li>
	<li>SA → ME: Negotiate C cart.</li>
	<li>ME: Signs CartMandate(C).</li>
	<li>SA → CP: Request payment options.</li>
	<li>CP: Returns token (encrypted).</li>
	<li>SA: Presents mandate to U on trusted surface (e.g., GMSCore DPC).</li>
	<li>U: Signs Mandates (Sig_U).</li>
	<li>SA → CP: Sends PaymentMandate.</li>
	<li>MPP: Initiates payment with issuer, appending AI signals.</li>
</ol>

<p><strong>Human-Not-Present Flow:</strong></p>

<ol>
	<li>U signs IntentMandate pre-transaction.</li>
	<li>SA monitors (e.g., price drop via MCP tools).</li>
	<li>SA negotiates; ME validates against intent.</li>
	<li>If variable (e.g., shipping), escalate to U for CartMandate (force-present) [1].</li>
	<li>Proceed as above; PaymentMandate includes Not-Present flag.</li>
</ol>

<p><code>val mandate = A2aMessageBuilder().buildCartMandate(cart)  // User's device signs</code></p>

<p><code>DpcHelper.signMandate(mandate)  // Hardware-backed</code></p>

<p><code>Challenges (e.g., 3DS2) trigger U interactions; OTP relays via SA [1].</code></p>

<h3 style="font-size:1.8em;font-weight:700;">MAESTRO Framework: Layered Threat Modeling for AP2</h3>

<p>To complement STRIDE's application-focused threats, we apply MAESTRO [24], the Cloud Security Alliance's seven-layer framework for agentic AI ecosystems. MAESTRO uncovers multi-agent dynamics, emergent behaviors, and cross-layer dependencies unique to autonomous systems like AP2's Shopping Agents and Merchant Endpoints. Unlike STRIDE, which may overlook dynamic agent behaviors (e.g., emergent collusion), MAESTRO maps threats from foundational AI to ecosystem interactions, revealing risks in AP2's agentic architecture.</p>

<p> </p>

<h4 style="font-size:1.7em;font-weight:300;">Layer 1: Foundation Models</h4>

<p>STRIDE misses model-centric AI threats. In AP2, agents like ShoppingAgent (powered by foundation model) face targeted attacks.</p>

<ul>
	<li><strong>Emergent Decision Biases:</strong> Adversarial fine-tuning manipulates LLM outputs, causing ShoppingAgent to select sub-optimal products (e.g., biased towards malicious merchants).</li>
	<li><strong>Model Poisoning via Feedback Loops:</strong> Intent Mandates from users could indirectly poison model retraining, leading to persistent misinterpretation of shopping prompts.</li>
	<li><strong>Cross-Layer Impact:</strong> Biased decisions propagate to Layer 3, corrupting Cart Mandate generation.</li>
</ul>

<p>Mitigations: Adversarial training; model watermarking for signature integrity in mandates.</p>

<p> </p>

<h4 style="font-size:1.7em;font-weight:300;">Layer 2: Data Operations</h4>

<p>STRIDE covers data tampering but not RAG/vector database exploits, critical in AP2's context-aware flows.</p>

<ul>
	<li><strong>Memory Poisoning in Embedding Spaces:</strong> Corrupting agent memory (e.g., past carts via DpcHelper) influences retrieval, leading to false intent understanding in sub-agents like PaymentMethodCollector.</li>
	<li><strong>Semantic Attacks on Ontologies:</strong> Manipulating product knowledge bases causes agents to negotiate erroneous deals, enabling misappropriation in human-not-present modes.</li>
	<li><strong>Unique MAESTRO Threat: Temporal Data Drift:</strong> Agents learn from historical transactions; gradual poisoning creates emergent fraudulent patterns over time.</li>
</ul>

<p>Mitigations: Query validation; isolated vector databases per role.</p>

<p> </p>

<h4 style="font-size:1.7em;font-weight:300;">Layer 3: Agent Frameworks</h4>

<p>STRIDE's spoofing applies, but MAESTRO reveals autonomy-specific risks in AP2's orchestration.</p>

<ul>
	<li><strong>Workflow Hijacking via Prompt Injection:</strong> Compromised instructions redirect agent delegation (e.g., from shopper sub-agent to malicious endpoints), bypassing Intent Mandate checks.</li>
	<li><strong>Emergent Goal Misalignment:</strong> Sub-agents colluding autonomously to minimize authentication (e.g., PaymentMethodCollector ignoring high-risk merchants).</li>
	<li><strong>Logic Bomb Activation:</strong> Time-triggered behaviors in Cart Mandate validation, e.g., approving high-value txns during off-hours.</li>
</ul>

<p>Mitigations: Sandboxed execution; on-device verification in Android samples.</p>

<p> </p>

<h4 style="font-size:1.7em;font-weight:300;">Layer 4: Deployment Infrastructure</h4>

<p>STRIDE addresses infrastructure, but MAESTRO highlights agent container dynamics.</p>

<ul>
	<li><strong>Container Escape Leading to Agent Collusion:</strong> Escaped containers enable malicious agents to coordinate DDoS on merchant servers, exploiting shared A2A channels.</li>
	<li><strong>Service Mesh Poisoning for Inter-Agent Routing:</strong> Redirecting communications disrupts mandate flows, e.g., Payment Mandates routed to fake issuers.</li>
	<li><strong>Cross-Layer Vulnerability: Instrumentation Blindspots:</strong> Over-reliance on Kubernetes monitoring misses sub-agent isolation failures.</li>
</ul>

<p>Mitigations: Micro-segmentation; immutable containers for agents.</p>

<p> </p>

<h4 style="font-size:1.7em;font-weight:300;">Layer 5: Evaluation and Observability</h4>

<p>STRIDE's info disclosure applies to logs, but MAESTRO uncovers HITL fatigue in AP2's autonomous txns.</p>

<ul>
	<li><strong>Anomaly Flooding in Behavioral Monitoring:</strong> Agents generating false positives overwhelm reviewers, enabling slow cartel attacks across purchases.</li>
	<li><strong>Log Injection Hiding Coordinating Attacks:</strong> Malicious agents alter audit trails to mask cartel coordination (e.g., multiple CPs sharing compromised tokens).</li>
	<li><strong>Unique Threat: Observability Bypass via Emergent Behaviors:</strong> Subjective decisions blending normal patterns, evading dashboards.</li>
</ul>

<p>Mitigations: AI-powered anomaly correlation; decentralized logging.</p>

<p> </p>

<h4 style="font-size:1.7em;font-weight:300;">Layer 6: Security and Compliance</h4>

<p>STRIDE includes elevation, but MAESTRO exposes policy reinterpretation in dynamic agents.</p>

<ul>
	<li><strong>Policy Manipulation in Agent Reasoning:</strong> Compromised agents exploit LLM flexibility to reinterpret SCA rules, e.g., bypassing 3DS for "trusted" collaborators.</li>
	<li><strong>Compliance Blind Spots in Multi-Agent Governance:</strong> Agents collectively evading PSD2 by distributing violations across roles.</li>
	<li><strong>Risk: Adaptive Policy Evasion:</strong> Agents learning from rejections to create emergent bypassing strategies.</li>
</ul>

<p>Mitigations: Formal policy verification; runtime guardrails.</p>

<p> </p>

<h4 style="font-size:1.7em;font-weight:300;">Layer 7: Agent Ecosystem</h4>

<p>STRIDE covers communication, but MAESTRO delves into trust ecosystems.</p>

<ul>
	<li><strong>Agent Impersonation in A2A Protocols:</strong> Fake Merchant Endpoints signing invalid Cart Mandates, establishing false trust.</li>
	<li><strong>Emergent Ecosystem Collusion:</strong> Multiple agents coordinating to manipulate markets (e.g., inflating prices via puppeteered negotiations).</li>
	<li><strong>Communication Protocol Exploitation:</strong> MITM in MCP tool calls, hijacking credential flows in Payment Mandates.</li>
	<li><strong>Unique MAESTRO Risk: Reputation Exploitation:</strong> Agents manipulating trust scores to prioritize compromised peers.</li>
</ul>

<p>Mitigations: DID-based agent identities [9]; zero-trust A2A channels.</p>

<p> </p>

<h3 style="font-size:1.8em;font-weight:700;">Cryptographic Foundations and Proofs</h3>

<p>AP2's security relies on digital signatures for non-repudiation. Formally:</p>

<ul>
	<li>Let M be a mandate, K_U private key.</li>
	<li>Sig_U(M) = ECDSA.Sign(K_U, Hash(M)).</li>
	<li>Verification: ECDSA.Verify(Pub_K_U, Hash(M), Sig_U(M)) → Boolean.</li>
</ul>

<p>Weakness: Quantum threats [19]; future AP2 versions recommend hybrid schemes.</p>

<p><strong>Privacy:</strong> Role separation ensures SA never sees raw credentials; CP returns tokens only.</p>

<h2 style="font-size:2.2em;font-weight:400;">Secure Usage Guidelines</h2>

<h3 style="font-size:1.8em;font-weight:700;">Implementation Best Practices</h3>

<p><strong>1. Key Management:</strong> Use TPM/HSM for signing. Rotate keys every 90 days; revoke compromised keys via DID methods [9].</p>

<p><strong>2. Mandate Validation:</strong> Pre-transaction: Verify merchant signatures. Post-signing: Check hashes match.</p>

<p><strong>3. Registry Setup:</strong> Build allowlists using Ethereum-like ledgers for agents.</p>

<p><strong>4. Encryption:</strong> AES-GCM-256 for mandate payloads; PGP for cross-role transfers.</p>

<p><strong>5. Step-Up Protocols:</strong> Integrate 3DS2; for Android, leverage GMSCore DPC for biometric confirmation.</p>

<p>Example: From Python samples, signing on device [1]:</p>

<p><code>def sign_mandates_on_user_device(cart_mandate, intent_mandate):</code></p>

<p><code>    # Assume device API</code></p>

<p><code>    signed_cart = device.sign(cart_mandate)</code></p>

<p><code>    return signed_cart</code></p>

<p><strong>6. Logging:</strong> Store mandates in tamper-proof ledgers; include timestamps, agent IDs.</p>

	<li><strong>Human-Not-Present:</strong> Set conservative TTL (e.g., 24h); require multi-agent consensus for high-value.</li>
	<li><strong>Disputes:</strong> Parties share mandates; adjudicators verify signatures, per [1].</li>
